name: Casablanca
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Casablanca: counterparty and group ownership research, commercial court support and CFC entity diligence.
hero_lede: Investigative consulting for matters touching Casablanca, scoped from Nashville: research on Moroccan groups and Casablanca Finance City entities, factual support for counsel before the city's commercial courts and arbitration centre, and diligence on counterparties connected to Morocco's main port, banking centre and stock exchange.
intro: Casablanca is Morocco's commercial and financial capital. The city recorded 3.22 million residents in the 2024 census, with around 4.27 million in Greater Casablanca. Its port is one of the largest artificial ports in Africa, and Mohammed V International Airport is the country's principal international gateway. The Casablanca Stock Exchange is among Africa's largest by market capitalisation, and the city hosts the headquarters of major banks including Attijariwafa Bank, BCP Group and Bank of Africa. The wider Casablanca region concentrates a large share of the country's industrial production, from food processing, textiles and building materials to electronics. Casablanca Finance City, created by law in 2010, offers an incentive status to companies serving Africa.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Casablanca because so much Moroccan corporate decision-making, finance and trade passes through it. Investors and lenders need to understand family-controlled groups whose holdings span banking, real estate, distribution and industry. Multinationals using Casablanca Finance City as a platform for African operations want to know who stands behind regional partners and intermediaries. Exporters, importers and logistics firms face documentary and payment disputes linked to the port. Disputes over contracts, insolvency and award enforcement come before the Casablanca commercial courts or are arbitrated at the Casablanca International Mediation and Arbitration Centre, where counsel need well-sourced facts on counterparties and their assets.

matters.title: Family group ownership mapping
matters.text: Tracing how Casablanca-based family groups hold their banking, distribution, real estate and industrial interests, using OMPIC company filings, stock exchange disclosures and press archives, so investors and lenders can see related parties, cross-guarantees and the people who actually take decisions.

matters.title: CFC partner and intermediary diligence
matters.text: Background research on companies holding Casablanca Finance City status and on the agents, advisers and regional partners they introduce, particularly where those intermediaries manage relationships in sub-Saharan African markets with elevated bribery and sanctions risk.

matters.title: Port trade and payment disputes
matters.text: Fact-finding for exporters, importers, insurers and trade-finance providers where shipments through the Port of Casablanca are disputed, documents appear inconsistent or buyers default, including research into the counterparties, their related companies and their history before the commercial courts.

matters.title: Commercial court litigation support
matters.text: Assembling factual records for counsel in contract, insolvency and enforcement proceedings before the Casablanca Commercial Court and Commercial Court of Appeal, including corporate histories, prior judgments located through lawful means, and publicly documented assets relevant to recovery.

matters.title: Real estate and developer research
matters.text: Checking the ownership, financing and dispute history of Casablanca property developers and landowning companies before acquisitions, joint developments or lending, and identifying whether nominee shareholders or related entities sit behind a project. Land title records are consulted through counsel where a legitimate interest exists.

local_context.title: Casablanca commercial courts
local_context.text: Casablanca has a specialised Commercial Court of first instance and one of Morocco's three Commercial Courts of Appeal, established under Law No. 53-95. They hear company, insolvency, banking and contract disputes and rule on the recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards. In the Ynna Holding v. Five FCB matter in 2015, the Casablanca Commercial Court granted exequatur of a foreign award, a decision often cited as evidence of a supportive approach to arbitration.

local_context.title: CIMAC arbitration and mediation
local_context.text: The Casablanca International Mediation and Arbitration Centre was established in 2016 at the initiative of the CGEM employers' confederation and the Casablanca Finance City Authority. Its rules draw on ICC and LCIA practice, it has an international arbitration court, and parties may conduct proceedings in French, English, Arabic or Spanish. It handles commercial disputes arising in Morocco, elsewhere in Africa and beyond. Investigative support is limited to factual research for counsel and the parties.

local_context.title: Casablanca Finance City
local_context.text: Casablanca Finance City was set up under a 2010 law to attract financial institutions, professional services firms and regional headquarters serving Africa. Eligible companies obtain CFC status, which brings tax benefits and a faster setup process, and members include multinational firms in finance, consulting and technology. CFC status indicates eligibility for the regime, not operational substance, so diligence still confirms staff, activity and ownership.

local_context.title: Business bodies and records
local_context.text: The CGEM, Morocco's main employers' confederation, is based in Casablanca and is a frequent source of sector context. Company legal records, articles and financial statements are obtained through OMPIC's national registry services rather than a city-specific registry, while the Casablanca Stock Exchange publishes listed issuers' disclosures, which are often the most detailed public source on large Moroccan groups. Searches are therefore planned around OMPIC and exchange sources first.

tdsc_approach: For matters touching Casablanca, TDSC begins by defining the question, such as who controls a family group, whether a CFC-based partner has real substance, or what assets a debtor holds, and then identifies the Casablanca sources that answer it. Research is conducted from Nashville using OMPIC filings, stock exchange disclosures, French- and Arabic-language press and published court material. Where document retrieval at the commercial court or interviews are justified, TDSC coordinates with qualified local professionals and the client's Moroccan counsel, who confirm the methods are lawful. Personal data is handled with Law 09-08 in mind, and transfers outside Morocco are reviewed with counsel before they occur.

faqs.q: How do you research a Casablanca family-owned group?
faqs.a: We start with OMPIC registry filings for each known entity, then work outward through shareholders, directors and financial statements, stock exchange disclosures where any group company is listed, and French- and Arabic-language press. The result is a map of related companies and decision-makers, with gaps clearly marked where filings are incomplete or holdings run through foreign vehicles.

faqs.q: Does Casablanca Finance City status confirm a company is substantial?
faqs.a: No. CFC status shows a company qualified for the regime and its incentives, but it does not establish how many people it employs, what business it actually conducts or who ultimately owns it. We test those points separately through filings, public footprint and, where justified, enquiries made by qualified local professionals.

faqs.q: Can you support an arbitration at CIMAC or enforcement in Casablanca?
faqs.a: Yes, by providing factual research to counsel. That can include the opposing party's corporate structure, related companies, assets documented in public sources and previous disputes. Applications to the Casablanca Commercial Court for exequatur or enforcement are handled by Moroccan counsel; our work supplies the factual basis they need.

faqs.q: Which languages do Casablanca records and sources use?
faqs.a: Company filings and court documents are generally in Arabic or French, business press is largely French, and some listed companies publish in English. We review sources in their original language and note where translation affects meaning, which matters for names that are transliterated in several ways.

faqs.q: Does TDSC have an office in Casablanca?
faqs.a: No. TDSC is based in Nashville and has no office or staff in Casablanca or elsewhere in Morocco. Most of our work is desk-based research. Where on-the-ground steps are required, we coordinate with qualified local professionals working lawfully and alongside the client's Moroccan counsel. We decline covert or restricted methods.
